newsitem.title: USA: Rockwell sees strong growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Rockwell sees strong growth in 1997.

text.p: Rockwell International Corp said on Wednesday it expects strong earnings growth in fiscal 1997.

Rockwell said it expects its Semiconductor Systems business, which had fourth quarter earnings 55 percent above the year-ago period, will maintain its 1996 earnings growth. The unit makes personal computer and fax modem chipsets.
Rockwell also said a strong commercial air transport market will allow earnings growth for avionics and communications while its automation and automotive units are also seen growing in 1997.

"We have set an objective of increasing our sights on earnings growth up to 15 percent," said Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Donald Beall in an interview. "It used to be in the low double-digits. Our growth will be driven by our electronics businesses."

Earlier Rockwell reported fourth quarter earnings fell to $97 million or $0.45 a share from $189 million or $0.88 a share a year earlier. Excluding special charges, profits from continuing operations rose to $0.88 a share compared with $0.53 a share in the year-ago period.

During the quarter Rockwell laid off 1,400 workers primarily in its automotive operations overseas. Beall said the move was aimed at "simply improving efficiency in certain businesses and plants." He declined comment on whether further lay-offs were planned.
Following the sale of its aerospace and defense businesses to Boeing Co, Beall said Rockwell would be in a position to make strategic acquisitions.
"We are looking at external and internal investments in all of these businesses but I'm not forecasting anything," Beall said.

Even without any acquisitions, Beall said, the company can still meet or beat its own earnings targets and its goal to improve revenues at eight percent annually. "I wouldn't want anyone to think we have to rush out and make an acquisition."
"I certainly wouldn't expect Rockwell to get into a whole new line of business, we've got lots of opportunities with the businesses we're in," he added.
Beall said Rockwell has no plans at the moment for any other major divestitures or sale of assets.

With the pending sale of its aerospace and defense businesses to Boeing, Rockwell seems to be nearing the end of a transformation in a little over a decade from a defense company working for government dollars to a diversified commercial enterprise.

U.S. government dollars only account for six percent of revenues compared with 63 percent in 1984. Electronics, which now accounts for 70 percent of revenues, is viewed by Beall as the jewel in the crown of the new-look Rockwell.
Beall said he would continue to push for enhancing shareholder value in fiscal 1997. The company previously said it plans to repurchase $1 billion of its common stock.
Shares of Rockwell were 1-5/8 higher at 56-1/2 in early afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
